notes.decision: Treated triple ⲛⲁ as decorative chapter-heading sigla framing the title, parallel to the > < marks bracketing the running title in the header. Rendered as ‹ ... › quotation guillemets.

Greek ἀρετή 'virtue, excellence.' Chapter title 'Concerning the Virtue of the Firmaments' — ⲁⲣⲉⲧⲏ here designates the cosmic-functional excellence/power of the firmaments as established by the Living Spirit's rich son.

Lycopolitan verbal form of 'receive/take' (paralleled by line 19 ⲁϩⲧ ⲁⲧⲟⲟⲧϥ 'received into his hand'). Probable reduced form of ⲁⲙⲁϩⲧⲉ 'grasp, take hold' or related receiving-verb. Translated 'received' for both occurrences.

Greek ἀπαρχή 'firstfruits.' Cosmogonic technical term: 'the firstfruits of his Five Sons' = the captured light-elements taken by the dark powers in the primordial battle, paralleling 'the firstfruits of the firmaments' in line 19-20.

ⲭⲁⲗⲭ = Lyc. reflex of ϫⲱⲗϫ 'mingle, twist together' (in accumulated vocab); ⲣ̄-ⲥⲧⲁⲩⲣⲉ = σταυρόω 'crucify.' The cosmic crucifixion of the archontic host — they are bound and stretched out across the cosmic frame, mingled with the captured light. Manichaean technical motif of the cosmic cross.

ⲣⲁⲡⲡⲉ tentatively rendered 'their members' on contextual grounds (the archontic host being mingled and dispersed); etymology unclear, possibly Lyc. variant of ⲣⲱⲡⲉ 'limb' or related body-part term. ⲟⲩⲁⲧϩ̄ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ likely = ⲟⲩⲱⲧⲡ̄ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ 'pour/transfer forth.' The whole reading is provisional.

'A rich one in power' — the rich son of the Living Spirit. ⲧⲟⲁⲙ = ϫⲟⲙ 'power' (Lyc.). The 'rich one in power' is the cosmic figure commissioned to set up the firmaments — likely identifiable with one of the Five Sons of the Living Spirit (possibly the King of Honor or the Great Builder).

notes.coptic_form: ⲧⲛ[ⲧⲁⲛⲧ] ⲙⲡⲓⲣⲏⲧⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧϩⲉ ... ⲙⲛ̄ ⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛⲁⲣⲭⲓⲧⲉⲕⲧⲱⲛ
notes.decision: The Living Spirit being likened to a human architect who builds the king's house — standard Manichaean cosmogonic typology where the cosmic Builder corresponds to the earthly architect. The simile continues into the architectural details (houses, exedrae) of lines 29-31.
Likely Greek ἐξέδρα 'exedra, outer/recessed room' adapted to Coptic with ⲁϩⲛ- prefix (= ⲁϩⲟⲩⲛ 'into'). Architectural term fitting the king's-house simile. Translated 'outer rooms.'
Translated 'Father of Life' — standard Manichaean cosmogonic title for the high Father in his life-giving aspect. Recurs at line 22.

Doublet 'wise craftsman, an artisan' — ⲍⲁⲙϣⲉ + ⲛⲥⲁⲃⲉ (native Coptic 'wise craftsman') paralleled with Greek τεχνίτης 'artisan' as parable-establishing figure. The Father is being likened to such a one.
Translated 'thoughtfulness' — ⲙⲛⲧ-ⲣⲙ̄ⲛϩⲏⲧ literally 'state-of-thoughtful-person.' Distinct from ⲡⲱⲕ ⲛⲍⲏⲧ 'purpose of heart' and from ⲙⲛⲧⲍⲏⲧⲥⲛⲉⲩ 'double-mindedness.'
Read as Lycopolitan ⲙⲟⲩϩ 'fill, filling.' Recurs in line 14-15 and possibly line 18. The craftsman's filling/casting action in the crucible. Confidence moderate.

Translated 'crucible of melting' — ⲃⲁⲡ likely a smelting-vessel (possibly Greek βαφή 'dipping/dyeing-vat,' or related to ⲃⲁⲡϩ 'striking down'); ⲥⲗⲱⲃⲗⲱⲃϩ reduplicated form of ⲗⲱⲃϣ 'mingle/blend' (in glossary), giving 'molten state, melting.' Fits the metallurgical phase of craftsman-imagery alongside woodworking.

Rendered as 'jars, bowls, lids' — list of wooden vessel types. ⲕⲉⲃⲁⲭⲟⲥ likely a Greek-derived vessel-name (possibly κάδος 'jar' or κήβος); ⲫⲓⲁⲗⲏ = phiale/bowl (Greek); ⲭⲁⲡ possibly 'lid/cover' (cf. ϫⲁⲡ). Listing certain vessel types.

Greek loanword ἀργόν 'idle, unworked, raw' — describes the wood in its uncrafted state, prior to the craftsman's shaping. Captures the parable's contrast between raw material and finished useful vessel.

Translated 'imprint' (in glossary as 'seal/imprint') — the unworked wood has no shaping-imprint upon it yet. Standard Manichaean correspondential vocabulary for the typological shaping-mark of the craftsman.
Read as ⲛ̄-ⲛⲁϩⲣⲛ̄-ⲧⲟⲟⲧϥ̄ 'in his hand/at his disposal' — the craftsman's wisdom is operative in his hand (i.e. his execution). Lycopolitan compound preposition.

'Third Ambassador' — the standard Manichaean title (tertius legatus, in glossary). Identified here as 'the great king' who comes to dwell in the cosmos, parallel to the parable-king who comes to receive vessels from his craftsman.

Translated 'down to the Deep' though the glossary lists ⲁⲍⲣⲏⲓ̈ as 'upward.' Coptic ⲉϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ is famously dual-sense (up/down), and with ⲡⲛⲟⲩⲛ ('the Deep, abyss') the verb ⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ ('cast') requires downward direction. The descent of Error and Darkness to the abyss is the standard Manichaean cosmological terminus.
